{{About|Eulerian circles of set theory and logic|the geometric Euler circle|Nine-point circle}}
[[File:EulerDiagram.svg|thumb|Euler diagram illustrating that the set of "animals with four legs" is a subset of "animals", but the set of "minerals" is a disjoint set (it has no members in common) with "animals"]]
[[File:Euler diagram of solar system bodies.svg|thumb|300x300px|Euler diagram showing the relationships between different [[Solar System]] objects]]
An '''Euler diagram''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɔɪ|l|ər}}, {{respell|OY|lər}}) is a [[diagram]]matic means of representing [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] and their relationships. They are particularly useful for explaining complex hierarchies and overlapping definitions. They are similar to another set diagramming technique, [[Venn diagram]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Moktefi |first1=A. |last2=Lemanski |first2=J. |date=2022-12-01 |title=On the Origin of Venn Diagrams |journal=Axiomathes |language=en |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=887–900 |doi=10.1007/s10516-022-09642-2 |issn=1572-8390|doi-access=free }}</ref> Unlike Venn diagrams, which show all possible relations between different sets, the Euler diagram shows only relevant relationships.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Moktefi |first1=Amirouche |last2=Shin |first2=Sun-Joo |title=A History of Logic Diagrams |date=2012-01-01 |series=Handbook of the History of Logic |volume=11 |pages=611–682 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/chapter/handbook/abs/pii/B9780444529374500113 |access-date=2025-11-18 |publisher=North-Holland |doi=10.1016/B978-0-444-52937-4.50011-3 |isbn=978-0-444-52937-4 |language=en-US|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The Swiss mathematician [[Leonhard Euler]] (1707–1783) is one of the most important authors in the history of this type of diagram, but he is only the namesake, not the inventor. Euler diagrams were first developed for logic, especially [[Syllogism|syllogistics]], and only later transferred to set theory.  In the United States, both Venn and Euler diagrams were incorporated as part of instruction in [[set theory]] as part of the [[new math]] movement of the 1960s. Since then, they have also been adopted by other curriculum fields such as reading<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.readingquest.org/strat/venn.html |title=Strategies for Reading Comprehension Venn Diagrams |access-date=2009-06-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090429093334/http://readingquest.org/strat/venn.html |archive-date=2009-04-29 |url-status=dead }}</ref> as well as organizations and businesses.

Euler diagrams consist of simple closed shapes in a two-dimensional plane that each depict a set or category. How or whether these shapes overlap demonstrates the relationships between the sets. Each curve divides the plane into two regions or "zones": the interior, which symbolically represents the [[element (mathematics)|element]]s of the set, and the exterior, which represents all elements that are not members of the set. Curves which do not overlap represent [[disjoint sets]], which have no elements in common. Two curves that overlap represent sets that [[intersection (set theory)|intersect]], that have common elements; the zone inside both curves represents the set of elements common to both sets (the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the sets). A curve completely within the interior of another is a [[subset]] of it.

== History ==
Diagrams reminiscent of Euler diagrams and with similar functions seem to have existed for a long time.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lemanski |first=J. |url=https://philarchive.org/rec/LEMWAL-2 |title=World and Logic |date=2021 |publisher=College Publications |isbn=9781848903845 |location=London |pages=182–196}}</ref> However, exact dates for these diagrams can only be determined historically after the invention of [[printing press]].

=== Before Euler ===
The first authors to print an Euler-esque diagram and briefly discuss it in their texts were [[Juan Luis Vives]] (in 1531), [[Nicolaus Reimers]] (in 1589), [[Bartholomäus Keckermann]] (in 1601) and [[Johann Heinrich Alsted]] (in 1614).<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Lemanski |first=J. |date=2017 |title=Periods in the Use of Euler-Type Diagrams |url=https://philarchive.org/rec/LEMPIT |journal=Acta Baltica Historiae et Philosophiae Scientiarum |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=50–69 |doi=10.11590/abhps.2017.1.03|doi-access=free }}</ref> The first detailed elaboration of these diagrams can be traced back to [[Erhard Weigel]] (1625–1699), who called this type of diagram a 'logometrum' (a measuring instrument for logic).<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Lemanski |first=J. |date=2018-01-02 |title=Logic Diagrams in the Weigel and Weise Circles |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/01445340.2017.1341074 |journal=History and Philosophy of Logic |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=3–28 |doi=10.1080/01445340.2017.1341074 |issn=0144-5340|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Weigel was the first to prove all valid syllogisms with the aid of shapes in a two-dimensional plane. In the case of generally affirmative judgements (all-sentences), the geometric shape for the subject should lie completely within the shape for the predicate. In the case of negative judgements (no-sentences), it should lie completely outside. In the case of particular judgements (sentences with 'some', 'some...not'), the geometric shapes should partially overlap and not overlap. To prove a syllogism, one must first draw all possible figures for the premises and then see whether one can also read the conclusion from them. If this is the case, the syllogism is valid; otherwise, it is invalid.

Erhard Weigel used initial letters to represent the diagrams, whereas his students, such as  [[Johann Sturm|Johann Christoph Sturm]] (1635–1703) and [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] (1646–1716), used circles or lines.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lenzen |first=W. |title=Leibniz: Logic {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/leib-log/ |access-date=2025-11-18 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Castro-Manzano |first=J. M. |date=June 2017 |title=Re(dis)covering Leibniz's Diagrammatic Logic |url=http://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?script=sci_abstract&pid=S0188-66492017000100089&lng=es&nrm=iso&tlng=en |journal=Tópicos (México) |language=en |issue=52 |pages=89–116 |doi=10.21555/top.v0i52.760 |issn=0188-6649|doi-access=free }}</ref>  Another tradition can be traced back to [[Christian Weise]] (1642–1708), who is said to have used these diagrams in his teaching.<ref name=":1" /> This is reported by his students Samuel Großer and Johann Christian Lange. Lange in particular went beyond syllogistics with these diagrams and worked with quantified predicates, for example.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lemanski |first=J. |date=2020-04-01 |title=Euler-type Diagrams and the Quantification of the Predicate |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10992-019-09522-y |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |language=en |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=401–416 |doi=10.1007/s10992-019-09522-y |issn=1573-0433|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Euler and the time after ===
In his ''[[Letters to a German Princess]]'', Euler focused solely on traditional syllogistics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moktefi |first=A. |date=2015 |title=Is Euler's Circle a Symbol or an Icon? |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/MOKIEC-2 |journal=Sign Systems Studies |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=597–615 |doi=10.12697/SSS.2015.43.4.14 |doi-access=free }}</ref> He further developed Weigel's approach and not only tested the validity of syllogisms, but also developed a method for drawing conclusions from premises.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bernhard |first=P. |title=Euler-Diagramme: Zur Morphologie einer Repräsentationsform in der Logik |url=https://brill.com/display/title/49098 |access-date=2025-11-18 |website=brill.com}}</ref> At the same time as Euler, [[Gottfried Ploucquet]] and [[Johann Heinrich Lambert]] also used similar diagrams.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bellucci |first1=F. |last2=Moktefi |first2=A. |last3=Pietarinen |first3=A. |date=2013 |contribution=Diagrammatic Autarchy: Linear Diagrams in the 17th and 18th Century|title=Diagrams, Logic and Cognition: Proceedings of the First International Workshop on Diagrams, Logic and Cognition|series=CEUR Workshop Proceedings|publisher= Sun SITE Central Europe, RWTH Aachen University |volume=1132|pages=31–35|contribution-url=http://ceur-ws.org/Vol-1132/paper4.pdf|access-date=2025-11-30}}</ref> However, the diagrams only became widely known in the 1790s through [[Immanuel Kant]] (1724–1804), who used them in his lectures on logic and his students then spread knowledge of the diagrams throughout Europe.<ref>{{Citation |last=Lu-Adler |first=H. |title=From Logical Calculus to Logical Formality - What Kant Did with Euler's Circles |date=2017 |work=Kant and his German contemporaries |pages=35–55 |editor-last=Dyck |editor-first=C. |url=https://philarchive.org/rec/LUAFLC |access-date=2025-11-18 |publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lemanski |first=J. |date=2024-03-01 |title=Kant's Crucial Contribution to Euler Diagrams |journal=Journal for General Philosophy of Science |language=en |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=59–78 |doi=10.1007/s10838-023-09653-6 |issn=1572-8587|doi-access=free }}</ref> In the 19th century, Euler diagrams became the most widely used form of representation in logic, esp. by 'Kantians' such as [[Arthur Schopenhauer]], [[Karl Christian Friedrich Krause]] or [[Sir William Hamilton, 9th Baronet|Sir William Hamilton]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Moktefi |first=A. |chapter=Schopenhauer's Eulerian Diagrams |date=2020 |title=Language, Logic, and Mathematics in Schopenhauer |series=Studies in Universal Logic |pages=111–127 |editor-last=Lemanski |editor-first=J. |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-33090-3_8 |access-date=2025-11-18 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-33090-3_8 |isbn=978-3-030-33090-3|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kittsteiner |first=C. |chapter=Schopenhauer's Sorites Diagram |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2024 |volume=14981 |editor-last=Lemanski |editor-first=Jens |editor2-last=Johansen |editor2-first=Mikkel Willum |editor3-last=Manalo |editor3-first=Emmanuel |editor4-last=Viana |editor4-first=Petrucio |editor5-last=Bhattacharjee |editor5-first=Reetu |editor6-last=Burns |editor6-first=Richard |title=Diagrammatic Representation and |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-71291-3_12 |isbn=978-3-031-71291-3}}</ref>[[File:Hamilton Lectures on Logic 1874 Euler Diagrams.png|thumb|344x344px|A page from Hamilton's ''Lectures on Logic;'' the symbols '''{{sc|A}}''', '''{{sc|E}}''', '''{{sc|I}}''', and '''{{sc|O}}''' refer to four types of categorical statement which can occur in a [[syllogism]] (see [[#a_e_i_o_u_descrs_anchor|descriptions, left]]) The small text to the left erroneously says: "The first employment of circular diagrams in logic improperly ascribed to Euler. To be found in Christian Weise", a book which was actually written by Johann Christian Lange.<ref name=Venn_1881/><ref name=Gailand_1967/>]]
[[File:Couturat 1914 and Venn assignments1.jpg|thumb|400px|right|The diagram to the right is from Couturat<ref name=Courant-1914/>{{rp|style=ama|p= 74}} in which he labels the 8&nbsp;regions of the Venn diagram. The modern name for the "regions" is ''[[minterm]]s''. They are shown in the diagram with the variables {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, and {{mvar|z}} per Venn's drawing. The symbolism is as follows: logical {{nobr| {{sc|AND}} [ '''&''' ] }} is represented by arithmetic multiplication, and the logical {{nobr| {{sc|NOT}} [ {{big|'''¬'''}} ] }} is represented by ⟨′⟩ after the variable, e.g. the region {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}′{{mvar|z}} is read as "({{sc|NOT}} {{mvar|x}}) {{sc|AND}} ({{sc|NOT}} {{mvar|y}}) {{sc|AND}} {{mvar|z}}" i.e. {{nobr| (¬ {{mvar|x}}) & (¬ {{mvar|y}}) & {{mvar|z}} .}}]]

[[File:Veitch and Karnaugh 3.jpg|thumb|300px|right|Both the Veitch diagram and Karnaugh map show all the [[minterms]], but the Veitch is not particularly useful for reduction of formulas. Observe the strong resemblance between the Venn and Karnaugh diagrams; the colors and the variables {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, and {{mvar|z}} are per Venn's example.]]
Since the history of the diagrams was only partially researched in the 19th century, most logicians attributed the diagrams to Euler, leading to numerous misunderstandings, some of which persist to this day. As shown in the illustration to the right, Sir William Hamilton erroneously asserted that the original use of the circles to "sensualize... the abstractions of logic"<ref name="Hamilton-1858-1860">{{cite book |first=W.R. |last=Hamilton |author-link=Sir William Hamilton, 9th Baronet |date=1858–1860 |title=Lectures on Metaphysics and Logic |page=180}}<!--{{efn|group="nb"|name=Mansel_Veitch_1860_credit_note}} --></ref> was not [[Leonhard Paul Euler|Euler]] but rather [[Christian Weise|Weise]];<ref>{{cite book |first=C. |last=Weise |author-link=Christian Weise |year=1712 |title=Nucleus Logicae Weisianae |language=la |trans-title=Weissian core of logic}} — Published 4&nbsp;years after Weise's death.</ref> however the latter book was actually written by Johann Christian Lange, rather than Weise.<ref name="Venn_1881" /><ref name="Gailand_1967" /> He references Euler's ''[[Letters to a German Princess]]''.<ref name="Euler-1791-1842">{{cite book |first=L.P. |last=Euler |author-link=Leonhard Paul Euler |orig-date=17 February 1791 |publication-date=1842 |title=Lettres a une Princesse d'Allemagne |language=fr |trans-title=Letters to a German Princess |title-link=Letters to a German Princess |section=Partie&nbsp;II, Lettre&nbsp;XXXV |editor=Cournot |editor-link=Antoine Augustin Cournot |pages=412–417}}</ref>{{efn|group="nb"|name=Mansel_Veitch_1860_credit_note|
By the time these lectures of Hamilton were published, Hamilton had died. His editors (marked by {{sc|ED}}.), responsible for most of the footnote text, were the logicians [[Henry Longueville Mansel]] and [[John Veitch (poet)|John Veitch]].
}}

{{anchor|a_e_i_o_u_descrs_anchor}} In Hamilton's illustration of the four [[categorical proposition]]s<ref name=Hamilton-1860-Jevons-1881/> which can occur in a [[syllogism]] as symbolized by the drawings '''{{sc|A}}''', '''{{sc|E}}''', '''{{sc|I}}''', and '''{{sc|O}}''' are:
: '''{{sc|A}}''': The ''Universal Affirmative''
:: Example: ''All metals are elements.''
: '''{{sc|E}}''': The ''Universal Negative''
:: Example: ''No metals are compound substances.''
: '''{{sc|I}}''': The ''Particular Affirmative''
:: Example: ''Some metals are brittle.''
: '''{{sc|O}}''': The ''Particular Negative''
:: Example: ''Some metals are not brittle.''<ref name=Hamilton-1860-Jevons-1881>{{harvp|Hamilton|1860|p=179}}; these examples are from {{harvp|Jevons|1880|pp= 71 ff}}.</ref>

=== Euler diagrams in the era of Venn ===
[[John Venn]] (1834–1923) comments on the remarkable prevalence of the Euler diagram:
: "... of the first sixty logical treatises, published during the last century or so, which were consulted for this purpose–somewhat at random, as they happened to be most accessible–it appeared that thirty four appealed to the aid of diagrams, nearly all of these making use of the [[Leonhard Paul Euler|Eulerian]] scheme."<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V>{{cite book |first=J. |last=Venn |author-link=John Venn |year=1881a |section=Chapter&nbsp;V – Diagrammatic representation |title=Symbolic Logic |page= 100, Footnote 1}}</ref>

[[File:Venn 1881 p 115-116 pasteup.jpg|thumb|300px|right|Composite of two pages from {{harvp|Venn|1881a|pp=115–116}} showing his example of how to convert a syllogism of three parts into his type of diagram; Venn calls the circles "Eulerian circles"{{refn|cf {{harvp|Sandifer|2004}} {{harvp|Venn|1881a|pp= 114 ff}};<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/> in the "Eulerian scheme" {{harvp|Venn|1881a|p= 100}}<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/> of "old-fashioned Eulerian diagrams" {{harvp|Venn|1881a|p= 113}}<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/>}}]]
But nevertheless, he contended, "the inapplicability of this scheme for the purposes of a really general logic"<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/>{{rp|style=ama|p= 100}} and then noted that,
: “It fits in, but badly, even with the four propositions of the common logic to which it is normally applied.”<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/>{{rp|style=ama|p= 101}}

Venn ends his chapter with the observation illustrated in the examples below—that their use is based on practice and intuition, not on a strict [[algorithm]]ic practice:
: “In fact ... those diagrams not only do not fit in with the ordinary scheme of propositions which they are employed to illustrate, but do not seem to have any recognized scheme of propositions to which they could be consistently affiliated.”<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/>{{rp|style=ama|pp= 124–125}}

Finally, in his Venn gets to a crucial criticism (italicized in the quote below); observe in Hamilton's illustration that the '''{{sc|O}}''' (''Particular Negative'') and '''{{sc|I}}''' (''Particular Affirmative'') are simply rotated:

: “We now come to Euler's well-known circles which were first described in his ''Lettres a une Princesse d'Allemagne'' (''Letters'' 102–105).<ref name=Euler-1791-1842/>{{rp|style=ama|pp= 102–105}} The weak point about these consists in the fact that they only illustrate in strictness the actual relations of classes to one another, rather than the imperfect knowledge of these relations which we may possess, or wish to convey, by means of the proposition. Accordingly they will not fit in with the propositions of common logic, but demand the constitution of a new group of appropriate elementary propositions. ... This defect must have been noticed from the first ''in the case of the particular affirmative and negative, for the same diagram is commonly employed to stand for them both, which it does indifferently well''”.[italics added]<ref name=Venn-1881b-§XX>{{cite book |first=J. |last=Venn |author-link=John Venn |year=1881b |section=Chapter&nbsp;XX – Historic notes |title=Symbolic Logic|page=424}}</ref><ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/>{{rp|style=ama|p= 100, Footnote 1}}{{efn|group="nb"|
{{harvp|Sandifer|2004}} points out that [[Leonhard Paul Euler|Euler]] himself also makes such observations: Euler reports that his figure&nbsp;45 (a simple intersection of two circles) has 4&nbsp;different interpretations.
}} 
Whatever the case, armed with these observations and criticisms, Venn<ref name=Venn-1881a-§V/>{{rp|style=ama|pp= 100–125}} then demonstrates how he derived what has become known as his [[Venn diagrams]] from the “...&nbsp;old-fashioned Euler diagrams.” In particular Venn gives an example, shown at the left.

By 1914, [[Louis Couturat|Couturat]] (1868–1914) had labeled the terms as shown on the drawing at the right.<ref name=Courant-1914/> Moreover, he had labeled the ''exterior region'' (shown as {{mvar|a}}′{{mvar|b}}′{{mvar|c}}′) as well. He succinctly explains how to use the diagram – one must ''strike out'' the regions that are to vanish:
:"Venn's method is translated in geometrical diagrams which represent all the constituents, so that, in order to obtain the result, we need only ''strike out (by shading)'' those which are made to vanish by the data of the problem."[italics added]<ref name=Courant-1914>{{harvp|Couturat|1914|pp= 73, 75}}</ref>{{rp|style=ama|p= 73}}

Given the Venn's assignments, then, the unshaded areas ''inside'' the circles can be summed to yield the following equation for Venn's example:
: "{{sc|No}} {{mvar|y}} is {{mvar|z}} and {{sc|ALL}} {{mvar|x}} is {{mvar|y}}: therefore {{sc|No}} {{mvar|x}} is {{mvar|z}}" has the equation {{nobr| {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}{{mvar|z}}′ + {{mvar|x}}{{mvar|y}}{{mvar|z}}′ + {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}′{{mvar|z}} }} for the unshaded area ''inside'' the circles (but this is not entirely correct; see the next paragraph).

In Venn the background surrounding the circles, does not appear: That is, the term marked "0", {{nobr| {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}′{{mvar|z}}′ .}}  Nowhere is it discussed or labeled, but Couturat corrects this in his drawing.<ref name=Courant-1914/> The correct equation must include this unshaded area shown in boldface:
: "{{sc|No}} {{mvar|y}} is {{mvar|z}} and {{sc|ALL}} {{mvar|x}} is {{mvar|y}}: therefore {{sc|No}} {{mvar|x}} is {{mvar|z}}" has the equation {{nobr| {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}{{mvar|z}}′ + {{mvar|x}}{{mvar|y}}{{mvar|z}}′ + {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}′{{mvar|z}} + ''' {{mvar|x}}′{{mvar|y}}′{{mvar|z}}′<nowiki/>'''.}}

In modern use, the Venn diagram includes a "box" that surrounds all the circles; this is called the universe of discourse or the [[domain of discourse]].

Couturat<ref name=Courant-1914/> observed that, in a direct [[algorithm]]ic (formal, systematic) manner, one cannot derive reduced Boolean equations, nor does it show how to arrive at the conclusion "{{sc|No}} {{mvar|x}} is {{mvar|z}}". Couturat concluded that the process "has ... serious inconveniences as a method for solving logical problems": 
:"It does not show how the data are exhibited by canceling certain constituents, nor does it show how to combine the remaining constituents so as to obtain the consequences sought. In short, it serves only to exhibit one single step in the argument, namely the equation of the problem; it dispenses neither with the previous steps, i. e., "throwing of the problem into an equation" and the transformation of the premises, nor with the subsequent steps, i. e., the combinations that lead to the various consequences. Hence it is of very little use, inasmuch as the constituents can be represented by algebraic symbols quite as well as by plane regions, and are much easier to deal with in this form."<ref name=Courant-1914/>{{rp|style=ama|p= 75}}

Thus the matter would rest until 1952 when [[Maurice Karnaugh]] (1924–2022) would adapt and expand a method proposed by [[Edward W. Veitch]]; this work would rely on the [[truth table]] method precisely defined by [[Emil Post]]<ref>{{cite thesis |first=E. |last=Post |author-link=Emil Post |year=1921 |degree=Ph.D. |title=Introduction to a general theory of elementary propositions}}</ref> and the application of propositional logic to switching logic by (among others) [[Claude Shannon|Shannon]], [[George Stibitz|Stibitz]], and [[Alan Turing|Turing]].{{efn|group="nb"|
See footnote in [[George Stibitz]] article.
}}
For example, Hill & Peterson (1968)<ref name=Hill-Peterson-1964-1968>{{cite book |author1=Hill |author2=Peterson |name-list-style=amp |orig-year=1964 |year=1968 |title=Boolean Algebra |chapter=Set theory as an example of Boolean algebra |at={{nobr|sections 4.5 ff}} }}</ref> present the Venn diagram with shading and all. They give examples of Venn diagrams to solve example switching-circuit problems, but end up with this statement:
::"For more than three variables, the basic illustrative form of the Venn diagram is inadequate. Extensions are possible, however, the most convenient of which is the Karnaugh map, to be discussed in Chapter 6."<ref name=Hill-Peterson-1964-1968/>{{rp|style=ama|p= 64}}
In Chapter 6, section 6.4 "Karnaugh map representation of Boolean functions" they begin with:
::"The Karnaugh map<sup>1</sup> [<sup>1</sup>Karnaugh 1953] is one of the most powerful tools in the repertory of the logic designer. ... A Karnaugh map may be regarded either as a pictorial form of a truth table or as an extension of the Venn diagram."<ref name=Hill-Peterson-1964-1968/>{{rp|style=ama|pp= 103–104}}

The history of Karnaugh's development of his "chart" or "map" method is obscure. The chain of citations becomes an academic game of "credit, credit; ¿who's got the credit?": {{harvp|Karnaugh|1953}} referenced {{harvp|Veitch|1952}}, Veitch, referenced {{harvp|Shannon|1938}},<ref>{{cite report |first=C.E. |last=Shannon |author-link=Claude E. Shannon |year=1938 |title={{grey|[no title cited]: In effect, Shannon's master's thesis}} |publisher=[[M.I.T.]]}}</ref> and {{harvp|Shannon|1938}}, in turn referenced (among other authors of logic texts) {{harvp|Couturat|1914}}. In Veitch's method the variables are arranged in a rectangle or square; as described in [[Karnaugh map]], Karnaugh in his method changed the order of the variables to correspond to what has become known as (the vertices of) a [[hypercube]].

=== Modern use of Euler diagrams ===
In the 1990s, Euler diagrams were developed as a logical system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hammer |first1=E. |last2=Shin |first2=S.-J. |date=1998-01-01 |title=Euler's visual logic |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/01445349808837293 |journal=History and Philosophy of Logic |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=1–29 |doi=10.1080/01445349808837293 |issn=0144-5340|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The cognitive advantages of the diagrams soon became apparent.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Shimojima |first=Atsushi |title=On the Efficacy of Representation |date=1996 |degree=PhD Thesis |publisher=Indiana University |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/SHIOTE-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cheng |first=P. C.-H. |date=2014-06-01 |title=Graphical notations for syllogisms: How alternative representations impact the accessibility of concepts |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1045926X13000517 |journal=Journal of Visual Languages & Computing |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=170–185 |doi=10.1016/j.jvlc.2013.08.008 |issn=1045-926X}}</ref> The diagrams were therefore not only used as set diagrams, but have since been used in many different ways and functions in computer science including artificial intelligence and software engineering, information technology, bioscience, medicine, economics, statistics and many other fields,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rodgers |first=P. |date=2014-06-01 |title=A survey of Euler diagrams |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1045926X13000499 |journal=Journal of Visual Languages & Computing |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=134–155 |doi=10.1016/j.jvlc.2013.08.006 |issn=1045-926X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and their philosophy and history have been discussed.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greaves |first=Mark |url=https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/P/bo3629060.html |title=The Philosophical Status of Diagrams |publisher=Center for the Study of Language and Information |series=Lecture Notes |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Shin |first1=S.-J. |title=Diagrams and Diagrammatical Reasoning |date=2025 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=E. N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2025/entries/diagrams/ |access-date=2025-11-18 |edition=Fall 2025 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Lemon |first2=Oliver |last3=Mumma |first3=John |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> In 2000, the conference series [https://diagrams-conference.org/previous-conferences The Theory and Application on Diagrams: An International Conference Series] began, which regularly addresses current research on Euler diagrams, among other topics.

== Relation between Euler and Venn diagrams ==
[[File:Syllogism-Set-Diagrams.svg|thumb|300px|right|Examples of small [[Venn diagram]]s ''(on left)'' showing how they can be easily transformed into equivalent Euler diagrams ''(right)''. In these, black shaded regions represent [[empty set]]s (to diagram universal quantification), red shaded regions with an x represent nonempty sets (to diagram existential quantification), and the other regions have not been specified as empty or non-empty.]]
[[Venn diagram]]s are a more restrictive form of Euler diagrams.  A Venn diagram must contain all 2<sup>''n''</sup> logically possible zones of overlap between its ''n'' curves, representing all combinations of inclusion/exclusion of its constituent sets.  Regions not part of the set are indicated by coloring them black, in contrast to Euler diagrams, where membership in the set is indicated by overlap as well as color.  When the number of sets grows beyond 3 a Venn diagram becomes visually complex, especially compared to the corresponding Euler diagram. The difference between Euler and Venn diagrams can be seen in the following example. Take the three sets:

* <math>A = \{1,\, 2,\, 5\}</math>
* <math>B = \{1,\, 6\}</math>
* <math>C = \{4,\, 7\}</math>

The Euler and the Venn diagrams of those sets are:

<gallery widths="300">
File:3-set Euler diagram.svg|Euler diagram
File:3-set Venn diagram.svg|Venn diagram
</gallery>

In a logical setting, one can use model-theoretic semantics to interpret Euler diagrams, within a [[universe of discourse]]. In the examples below, the Euler diagram depicts that the sets ''Animal'' and ''Mineral'' are disjoint since the corresponding curves are disjoint, and also that the set ''Four Legs'' is a subset of the set of ''Animal''s. The Venn diagram, which uses the same categories of ''Animal'', ''Mineral'', and ''Four Legs'', does not encapsulate these relationships. Traditionally the ''emptiness'' of a set in Venn diagrams is depicted by shading in the region. Euler diagrams represent ''emptiness'' either by shading or by the absence of a region.

Often a set of well-formedness conditions are imposed; these are topological or geometric constraints imposed on the structure of the diagram.  For example, connectedness of zones might be enforced, or concurrency of curves or multiple points might be banned, as might tangential intersection of curves. In the adjacent diagram, examples of small Venn diagrams are transformed into Euler diagrams by sequences of transformations; some of the intermediate diagrams have concurrency of curves. However, this sort of transformation of a Venn diagram with shading into an Euler diagram without shading is not always possible. There are examples of Euler diagrams with 9 sets that are not drawable using simple closed curves without the creation of unwanted zones since they would have to have non-planar dual graphs.

=== Example: Euler- to Venn-diagram and Karnaugh map ===
This example shows the Euler and Venn diagrams and Karnaugh map deriving and verifying the deduction "No ''X''s are ''Z''s".
In the illustration and table the following logical symbols are used:
* 1 can be read as "true", 0 as "false"
* ~ for NOT and abbreviated to ′ when illustrating the minterms e.g. x′ =<sub>defined</sub> NOT x,
* + for Boolean OR (from [[Boolean algebra (logic)|Boolean algebra]]: 0&nbsp;+&nbsp;0&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, 0&nbsp;+&nbsp;1&nbsp;=&nbsp;1&nbsp;+&nbsp;0&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, 1&nbsp;+&nbsp;1&nbsp;=&nbsp;1)
* & (logical AND) between propositions; in the minterms AND is omitted in a manner similar to arithmetic multiplication: e.g. x′y′z =<sub>defined</sub> ~x & ~y & z (From Boolean algebra: 0&sdot;0&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, 0&sdot;1 = 1&sdot;0 = 0, 1&sdot;1 = 1, where "&sdot;" is shown for clarity)
* → (logical IMPLICATION): read as IF ... THEN ..., or " IMPLIES ", ''P'' → ''Q'' =&nbsp;<sub>defined</sub> NOT ''P'' OR ''Q''

[[File:Veitch and Karnaugh truth table 4.jpg|thumb|921px|center|Before it can be presented in a Venn diagram or Karnaugh Map, the Euler diagram's syllogism "No ''Y'' is ''Z'', All ''X'' is ''Y''" must first be reworded into the more formal language of the [[propositional calculus]]: " 'It is not the case that: {{var|Y}} AND {{var|Z′}} AND 'If an {{var|X}} then a {{var|Y′}} ". Once the propositions are reduced to symbols and a propositional formula ( ~(y & z) & (x → y) ), one can construct the formula's [[truth table]]; from this table the Venn and/or the Karnaugh map are readily produced. By use of the adjacency of "1"s in the Karnaugh map (indicated by the grey ovals around terms 0 and 1 and around terms 2 and 6) one can "reduce" the example's [[Boolean equation]] i.e. (x′y′z′ + x′y′z) + (x′yz′ + xyz′) to just two terms: x′y′ + yz′. But the means for deducing the notion that "No X is Z", and just how the reduction relates to this deduction, is not forthcoming from this example.]]

Given a proposed conclusion such as "No ''X'' is a ''Z''", one can test whether or not it is a correct [[Deductive reasoning|deduction]] by use of a [[truth table]]. The easiest method is put the starting formula on the left (abbreviate it as ''P'') and put the (possible) deduction on the right (abbreviate it as ''Q'') and connect the two with [[logical implication]] i.e. ''P'' → ''Q'', read as IF ''P'' THEN ''Q''. If the evaluation of the truth table produces all 1s under the implication-sign (→, the so-called ''major connective'') then ''P'' → ''Q'' is a [[tautology (logic)|tautology]]. Given this fact, one can "detach" the formula on the right (abbreviated as ''Q'') in the manner described below the truth table.

Given the example above, the formula for the Euler and Venn diagrams is:
: "No ''Y''s are ''Z''s" and "All ''X''s are ''Y''s": ( ~(y & z) & (x → y) ) =<sub>defined</sub> ''P''
And the proposed deduction is:
: "No ''X''s are ''Z''s": ( ~ (x & z) ) =<sub>defined</sub> ''Q''

So now the formula to be evaluated can be abbreviated to:
: ( ~(y & z) & (x → y) ) → ( ~ (x & z) ): ''P'' → ''Q''
: IF ( "No ''Y''s are ''Z''s" and "All ''X''s are ''Y''s" ) THEN ( "No ''X''s are ''Z''s" )

At this point the above implication ''P'' → ''Q'' (i.e. ~(y & z) & (x → y) ) →  ~(x & z) ) is still a formula, and the deduction{{dash}}the "detachment" of ''Q'' out of ''P'' → ''Q''{{dash}}has not occurred. But given the demonstration that ''P'' → ''Q'' is tautology, the stage is now set for the use of the procedure of [[modus ponens]] to "detach" Q: "No ''X''s are ''Z''s" and dispense with the terms on the left.<ref group="nb">This is a sophisticated concept. Russell and Whitehead (2nd edition 1927) in their ''[[Principia Mathematica]]'' describe it this way: "The trust in inference is the belief that if the two former assertions [the premises P, P→Q ] are not in error, the final assertion is not in error . . . An inference is the dropping of a true premiss [sic]; it is the dissolution of an implication" (p. 9). Further discussion of this appears in "Primitive Ideas and Propositions" as the first of their "primitive propositions" (axioms): *1.1 Anything implied by a true elementary proposition is true" (p. 94). In a footnote the authors refer the reader back to Russell's 1903 ''Principles of Mathematics'' §38.</ref> 
 
''Modus ponens'' (or "the fundamental rule of inference"<ref>cf Reichenbach 1947:64</ref>) is often written as follows: The two terms on the left, ''P'' → ''Q'' and ''P'', are called ''premises'' (by convention linked by a comma), the symbol ⊢ means "yields" (in the sense of logical deduction), and the term on the right is called the ''conclusion'': 
: ''P'' → ''Q'', ''P'' ⊢ ''Q''

For the modus ponens to succeed, both premises ''P'' → ''Q'' and ''P'' must be ''true''. Because, as demonstrated above the premise ''P'' → ''Q'' is a tautology, "truth" is always the case no matter how x, y and z are valued, but "truth" is only the case for ''P'' in those circumstances when ''P'' evaluates as "true" (e.g. rows {{EquationNote|0}} OR {{EquationNote|1}} OR {{EquationNote|2}} OR {{EquationNote|6}}: x′y′z′ + x′y′z + x′yz′ + xyz′ = x′y′ + yz′).<ref group="nb">Reichenbach discusses the fact that the implication ''P'' → ''Q'' need not be a tautology (a so-called "tautological implication"). Even "simple" implication (connective or adjunctive) work, but only for those rows of the truth table that evaluate as true, cf Reichenbach 1947:64–66.</ref> 
: ''P'' → ''Q'', ''P'' ⊢ ''Q''
:* i.e.: ( ~(y & z) & (x → y) ) → ( ~ (x & z) ), ( ~(y & z) & (x → y) ) ⊢ ( ~ (x & z) )
:* i.e.: IF "No ''Y''s are ''Z''s" and "All ''X''s are ''Y''s" ''THEN'' "No ''X''s are ''Z''s", "No ''Y''s are ''Z''s" and "All ''X''s are ''Y''s" ⊢ "No ''X''s are ''Z''s"

One is now free to "detach" the conclusion "No ''X''s are ''Z''s", perhaps to use it in a subsequent deduction (or as a topic of conversation).

The use of tautological implication means that other possible deductions exist besides "No ''X''s are ''Z''s"; the criterion for a successful deduction is that the 1s under the sub-major connective on the right ''include'' all the 1s under the sub-major connective on the left (the ''major'' connective being the implication that results in the tautology). For example, in the truth table, on the right side of the implication (→, the major connective symbol) the bold-face column under the sub-major connective symbol " '''~''' " has all the same 1s that appear in the bold-faced column under the left-side sub-major connective '''&''' (rows {{EquationNote|0}}, {{EquationNote|1}}, {{EquationNote|2}} and {{EquationNote|6}}), plus two more (rows {{EquationNote|3}} and {{EquationNote|4}}).
